title: Why Penedès tastes the way it does

lede.text: Penedès sits in a young basin ringed by older mountains, under a Mediterranean climate. Its white grapes reach their best ripeness for these wines only here, and its whites are known for freshness, acidity and fruit.

chapters.title: A sunken basin between mountains
paras: The relief has three units. The Garraf massif and the pre-coastal range between Montserrat and the Montmell surround the Penedès pre-coastal depression. The oldest ground is in these mountain chains.

The depression itself is very young in geological terms. Before the Miocene, the Garraf and the pre-coastal range were one unit. After the depression sank, recent erosion by rivers and torrents sharpened the relief at its edges and carved deep ravines in the north of the area.
The production zone is made up of municipalities in two provinces, Barcelona and Tarragona. Ten smaller named areas, such as Massís del Garraf or Costers del Montmell, may be added to a label.

chapters.title: A Mediterranean climate with a day-night gap
paras: Penedès has a Mediterranean climate. In July and August the temperature differs between night and day.
Climate and soil, helped by that gap, allow red grapes to ripen well. They come out rich in anthocyanins and tannins, and in red-fruit aromas.

chapters.title: Deep, well-drained soils
paras: Active limestone runs between 5 and 10%. Soils are 40 cm to 120 cm or more deep, and most are between 80 and 120 cm. Drainage is generally good.
The surface texture is loam and silty loam. Between 1% and 5% of the soil at root depth is coarse stones.
A soil map decides which plots suit which grape.

chapters.title: Fresh whites, sparkling and sweet wines
paras: Penedès whites are known for their freshness, acidity and fruit. Its white grape varieties reach their best ripeness for these wines only in Penedès, where soil, climate and work come together. The rules allow 18 white varieties, Xarel·lo and Parellada among them. Ull de Llebre and Monastrell are among the 13 red varieties.
Yields are capped at 12,000 kg per hectare for white varieties and sparkling wine, and 9,000 kg for red varieties.

Whites smell of white and tropical fruit, and of ripe fruit if they have been in barrel. Rosados (rosé wines) range from pale pink to cherry in colour and smell of red fruit. Reds are garnet when young, and turn tawny red with age.

Sparkling wine is made by the traditional method, with at least 15 months from tirage to disgorging and a pressure of over 3.5 bar. It may also be made by the ancestral method, where the first fermentation is slowed or stopped so the grapes' own sugar drives the second, with no sugar or must added. The grapes and wine must be organic. By sugar it is labelled from Brut natural, under 3 g/l, to Dulce, over 50 g/l. Vino de aguja is a lightly sparkling wine, with a pressure of 1 to 2.5 bar.

Sweet wines come in four kinds. Vino dulce natural is a fortified wine made from overripe grapes of at least 240 g/l sugar, with alcohol added. Vino dulce de Malvasía de Sitges is also fortified, and is made only from the Malvasía de Sitges grape. Vino dulce de uva sobremadurada (overripe-grape sweet wine) is not fortified: it is made from overripe grapes with no artificial boost to strength. The fourth is the dulce de frío, in which cold stops fermentation and 70 to 150 g/l of sugar stays in the wine, with nothing added.
